oneLine: Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell sermon, urging a new generation to love the one God with all their heart and to live his covenant justly in the land he is giving them.

author.name: Moses (traditional); scribes of the late monarchy and exile (critical)
author.who: The book presents itself as Moses' speeches on the plains of Moab, written down and handed to the Levitical priests. Critical scholars see it as the product of a 'Deuteronomic' school of scribes, prophets and priests in Judah in the 7th century BC, expanded during the exile.
author.howWeKnow: Deut 1:1 introduces Moses' words, and Deut 31:9 and Deut 31:24 say Moses wrote this law down. The book is also framed by a narrator who speaks of Moses in the third person and records his death (Deut 34). Since de Wette (1805), critical scholars have linked the book's core (Deut 12-26) with the 'book of the law' found in the temple in 622 BC (2 Kgs 22:8), because Josiah's reform matches its demands: one central sanctuary, Passover in Jerusalem, removal of high places. Moshe Weinfeld showed close parallels with Assyrian loyalty oaths of the 7th century (especially Esarhaddon's succession treaty, 672 BC). Kenneth Kitchen and Meredith Kline argued instead that its overall shape matches 2nd-millennium Hittite treaties, supporting an earlier date.

writtenFrom.place: The plains of Moab, east of the Jordan (narrative setting)
writtenFrom.note: In the story, Moses speaks across from Jericho, within sight of the land he will not enter. On the critical view, the book was written in Jerusalem in the 7th century and completed in Babylonian exile, again with the land in view but out of reach.

writtenTo.who: The new generation about to enter Canaan; later, Judah under Josiah and the exiles
writtenTo.situation: A people standing between promise and possession must decide whether they will be loyal to the LORD alone in a land full of other gods. Moses' repeated 'today' (Deut 30:15-19) invites every generation that hears the book to stand in the same moment of decision.

setIn.note: The book covers about one month at the end of the fortieth year (Deut 1:3; Deut 34:8), c. 1406 BC on the early chronology or c. 1220 BC on the late. Critical scholars read the setting as literary, with the real audience living in the 7th-6th centuries BC.

worldEvents.event: Hittite kings such as Suppiluliuma I make vassal treaties with historical prologue, stipulations, deposit, reading, witnesses, blessings and curses.
Samaria falls to Assyria; northern refugees may have brought Deuteronomic traditions to Jerusalem.
Esarhaddon of Assyria imposes a loyalty oath on vassals, demanding they 'love' the crown prince with all their heart; its curses closely parallel Deut 28.
A 'book of the law' is found in the temple, and King Josiah launches a sweeping religious reform.
Jerusalem falls; Deuteronomy's warnings of exile come true, and its promise of return after repentance becomes the exiles' hope (Deut 30:1-5).

backdrop:
The name Deuteronomy comes from the Greek translation of Deut 17:18, where the king is to write 'a copy of this law'; the Greek translators rendered it *deuteronomion*, 'second law'. The book is not a new law but a retelling and application of the Sinai covenant for a generation about to settle down. Its Hebrew name, *Devarim*, means 'words', from its opening line.

Deuteronomy is shaped like an ancient treaty between a great king and a vassal people. It has a preamble (Deut 1:1-5), a history of what the great king has done (Deut 1-4), basic loyalty (Deut 5-11), detailed laws (Deut 12-26), blessings and curses (Deut 27-28), witnesses, and provisions for storing and reading the document (Deut 31:9-13). Ancient treaties demanded that vassals 'love' their overlord, meaning exclusive political loyalty. Deuteronomy uses that language for Israel's relationship with God: 'thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart' (Deut 6:5). Love here is not only feeling; it is wholehearted, practical loyalty. But it is also warmer than any treaty: God set his love on Israel because he loved them and kept his oath to their fathers (Deut 7:7-8).

The laws have a strong social conscience. Debts are released every seventh year (Deut 15:1-11), runaway slaves are not to be returned (Deut 23:15-16), workers are paid daily (Deut 24:14-15), and the 'stranger, the fatherless, and the widow' appear again and again (Deut 10:18; Deut 24:19-21). Even the king is limited: he must not multiply horses, wives or gold, and must read the law daily so that 'his heart be not lifted up above his brethren' (Deut 17:14-20). No other ancient law collection limits its king like this.

The book also has a unique demand: worship at 'the place which the LORD your God shall choose' (Deut 12:5), rather than at every local shrine. Critical scholars connect this with Josiah's centralisation of worship in Jerusalem. Traditional scholars note that the book never names Jerusalem and that it could refer to successive sanctuaries such as Shiloh. Either way, the demand protected Israel's worship from merging with the local cults of Canaan.

culture.explain: In ancient treaties, to 'love' the overlord meant to be loyal and obey him. Deuteronomy takes over this word for Israel's relationship with God, and fills it with warmth, gratitude and family language.
'Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD' (Deut 6:4). Recited twice daily by Jews, it confesses that the LORD alone is Israel's God and calls for undivided love.
Treaties ended with blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal, often in vivid lists. Deut 28's curses closely resemble those in Assyrian treaties. They apply to Israel as a nation in the land.
Treaties were stored in temples and read aloud regularly. Every seventh year at the feast of Booths, the whole people, including women, children and foreigners, were to hear the law read.

culture.term: The stranger, the fatherless and the widow
culture.explain: People without land or male protector were the most vulnerable in an agricultural, kinship-based society. Deuteronomy makes them the special concern of God and of every Israelite household.
Something 'devoted' was given wholly to God, often by destruction in war. Deuteronomy applies it to the Canaanite cities to remove idolatry. Its meaning and the scale it describes are debated.

jewishLens:
Deuteronomy gave Judaism its central confession. The Shema (Deut 6:4-9), along with Deut 11:13-21 and Num 15:37-41, is recited every morning and evening and, ideally, as the last words before death. Its commands are fulfilled literally: the words are written in the *mezuzah* fixed to doorposts and in the *tefillin* (phylacteries) bound on arm and forehead during morning prayer (Deut 6:8-9). A Jewish child's first verse is often 'Moses commanded us a law, even the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob' (Deut 33:4).

The rabbis also called Deuteronomy *Mishneh Torah*, 'repetition of the Torah', the name Maimonides later gave to his great law code. It is read in synagogue during the late summer, through the sad fast of Tisha B'Av and the 'seven weeks of comfort' toward the New Year, so that its warnings and promises of return frame Israel's season of repentance. The final verses, Moses' death and burial by God himself in an unknown grave (Deut 34:5-6), are read on Simchat Torah, when the cycle ends and begins again; the rabbis said the Torah begins with an act of kindness (God clothing Adam and Eve) and ends with one (God burying Moses).

The first audience would have heard Deuteronomy as a loving parent's last words. Moses keeps saying 'remember' and 'do not forget'. He insists that the law is not too hard or far away: 'the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it' (Deut 30:14). Obedience is the response of love to a God who chose Israel not because they were many or good but because he loved them (Deut 7:7-8; Deut 9:4-6). And he promises that even after exile, if Israel returns, God will gather them and 'circumcise thine heart' so they can love him fully (Deut 30:1-6).

flow.label: Remember the journey
flow.detail: Moses recalls forty years: the failure at Kadesh, the victories in Transjordan and God's faithfulness despite Israel's unbelief.

flow.label: Ten Words renewed
flow.detail: The covenant made at Horeb is restated for the new generation, which is now treated as standing there itself.

flow.label: Love the one LORD
flow.detail: The Shema and its explanation call for wholehearted loyalty, teaching children, and humility in prosperity.

flow.label: Laws for life in the land
flow.detail: One place of worship, festivals, debt release, just courts, limits on kings, care for the poor and fair treatment of workers and foreigners.

flow.label: Blessing or curse
flow.detail: A covenant ceremony at Shechem is commanded, with blessings for faithfulness and curses, including exile, for betrayal.

flow.label: Choose life
flow.detail: Moses foresees exile and return, promises a circumcised heart, and calls Israel to choose life today.

flow.label: Moses' song and death
flow.detail: Joshua is commissioned, Moses sings and blesses the tribes, views the land from Nebo and dies.

keyWords.meaning: To hear, listen and obey. In Hebrew, really hearing means responding.
Covenant loyalty with heart and action. God loves Israel first; Israel is to love God, the neighbour and the stranger.
To call to mind so that it shapes action. Israel remembers slavery and God's rescue, and acts justly.
The centre of thinking, choosing and feeling. Deuteronomy wants the law written on the heart, not only obeyed outwardly.
Teaching or instruction, like a parent's guidance; not merely legal code.
God chooses Israel and a place for his name; Israel must choose life.

connections.how: Joshua opens by applying Deuteronomy's call to be strong and courageous and to meditate on the law.
The book of the law found in Josiah's day, usually identified with Deuteronomy, drives his reform; Kings judges every king by Deuteronomy's standards.
Jeremiah's language is soaked in Deuteronomy, and he promises a new covenant with the law written on the heart.
Jesus answers all three wilderness temptations with words from Deuteronomy and names the Shema as the greatest commandment.
Peter and Stephen identify Jesus as the 'prophet like Moses' promised in Deut 18.
Paul reads Deut 30:12-14, 'the word is nigh thee', as the word of faith proclaimed in Christ.

jesusLens: Deuteronomy is one of the books Jesus quotes most. In the wilderness, as the true Israel tested forty days, he answers the devil three times from Deuteronomy (Matt 4:1-11; Deut 8:3; Deut 6:16; Deut 6:13), succeeding where the wilderness generation failed. He names the Shema as the first commandment (Mark 12:29-30). The early church saw him as the 'prophet like Moses' whom Israel must hear (Deut 18:15; Acts 3:22), and Paul reads the promise of a circumcised heart (Deut 30:6) as fulfilled by the Spirit (Rom 2:29). Paul also wrestles with Deuteronomy's curses, saying Christ became a curse for us by hanging on a tree (Gal 3:13; Deut 21:23). Jewish readers emphasise that Deuteronomy itself says the commandment is near and doable (Deut 30:11-14) and that it describes an ongoing relationship of love; Christian interpreters differ on how far Deuteronomy expects Israel to fail (Deut 31:16-29) and how that sets up the need for a new covenant.

misreadings.topic: Deuteronomy's blessings as a prosperity promise
misreadings.popular: Some prosperity preaching takes Deut 8:18 ('it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth') and Deut 28:1-14 as promises that any believer who obeys and gives faithfully will be financially rich and healthy.
misreadings.inContext: The blessings and curses belong to a national covenant tied to the land of Israel, in the form of an ancient treaty. They are corporate (the nation, its crops, its rain) and serve the covenant's goal of a just society where 'there shall be no poor among you' (Deut 15:4). Deut 8:18 is actually a warning against pride: when you are rich, remember it was God's gift, 'that he may establish his covenant'. Scholars such as Christopher Wright and Daniel Block stress this context.
misreadings.defence: Prosperity teachers argue that Gal 3:14 extends the blessing of Abraham to believers and that God still delights in providing. Evangelical scholars such as Gordon Fee (himself from a Pentecostal background) and D. A. Carson reply that the New Testament reinterprets blessing around the Spirit, contentment and generosity (1 Tim 6:6-10), and that the righteous often suffer (Job; Heb 11:35-38). Most agree that God does bless obedience, but not with a guaranteed financial formula.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Read in context, Deuteronomy's blessings call communities to generosity and justice; read as personal formulas, they can blame the poor and sick for their condition.

misreadings.topic: Love as feeling versus law as duty
misreadings.popular: The Old Testament demanded outward obedience to rules, while the New Testament introduced the idea of loving God from the heart.
misreadings.inContext: Deuteronomy is the Bible's great book of love. It commands love for God with all the heart (Deut 6:5), roots the law in God's prior love (Deut 7:7-8), calls Israel to circumcise its heart (Deut 10:16) and loves the stranger (Deut 10:19). Jesus' greatest commandment is a quotation of Deuteronomy. Scholars such as Jon Levenson (*The Love of God*, 2016) show how love and obedience belong together in covenant.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars agree, while noting that Deuteronomy itself anticipates Israel's failure (Deut 29:4; Deut 31:27-29) and promises that God will change the heart (Deut 30:6), a promise the New Testament sees fulfilled by the Spirit. So the difference between the covenants is not law versus love, but whether hearts are renewed.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Recognising love at the core of the Torah corrects a common caricature of Judaism and helps Christians see continuity between the Testaments.

relevance.then: Deuteronomy prepared Israel to keep faith in a land of abundance and rival gods: remember the rescue, love the LORD alone, build a just society, limit power, and know that unfaithfulness leads to exile while repentance leads home.
relevance.now: Deuteronomy shapes how believers think about love for God, memory, teaching children, justice for the poor and immigrants, the danger of comfort and the limits of political power. Its call to 'choose life' still confronts each generation.

sources.author: Jon D. Levenson
sources.title: The Love of God: Divine Gift, Human Gratitude, and Mutual Faithfulness in Judaism

oneLine: Joshua tells how God kept his promise of land, bringing Israel across the Jordan and into Canaan, and then asks each generation to choose whom it will serve.

author.name: Joshua and later editors (traditional); the Deuteronomistic historians (critical)
author.who: The Talmud credits Joshua with most of the book, with his death recorded by Eleazar and Phinehas (Baba Bathra 15a). Most critical scholars see Joshua as the first book of the Deuteronomistic History, written or edited in the late monarchy and exile using older stories and lists.
author.howWeKnow: Josh 24:26 says Joshua wrote words in the book of the law of God. The phrase 'unto this day' (Josh 4:9; Josh 7:26; Josh 15:63) shows a writer looking back on the events from some distance. The book's language and theology closely match Deuteronomy, which led Martin Noth (1943) to propose a single history running from Deuteronomy to Kings.
otherWritings: Part of the Deuteronomistic History: Judges, Samuel, Kings (critical view)

writtenFrom.note: On the critical view the book took shape in Jerusalem under Josiah (who also tried to reclaim and purify the land) and was finished in exile, when the land had been lost. Coordinates are for Jerusalem; the traditional view places composition in early Israel.

writtenTo.who: Israel as heirs of the promised land
writtenTo.place: Canaan; later Judah and the exiles
writtenTo.situation: Every generation needed to know that the land was a gift, not a conquest earned by strength, and that keeping it depended on loyalty to the LORD. For exiles who had lost the land, Joshua was both an explanation and a hope: God gave it once and can give it again.

setIn.note: From the Jordan crossing to Joshua's death at 110. Early chronology: c. 1406-1380 BC. Late chronology: c. 1230-1200 BC, the period when hundreds of new hill-country villages appear and when the Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC) first names Israel in Canaan. Many critical scholars think the book compresses a long, gradual process into a single campaign.

worldEvents.event: Amarna letters: Canaanite kings complain to Pharaoh about the 'Habiru', landless raiders destabilising the land.
Hazor's great Late Bronze palace is destroyed by an intense fire; the excavator Amnon Ben-Tor attributes it to the Israelites, others to Egyptians or internal revolt.
Pharaoh Merneptah's stele claims 'Israel is laid waste', showing Israel as a people in Canaan.
Around 300 small new villages appear in the central hill country, often linked with early Israel.
Josiah's reform and expansion northward; critical scholars see a Josianic edition of Joshua.

backdrop:
Canaan in the Late Bronze Age was a land of small, walled city-states, each with its own king, nominally under Egyptian control. The Amarna letters (14th century BC) show these kings quarrelling with each other and begging Egypt for troops. Around 1200 BC this world collapsed: cities burned, trade networks failed, and the Egyptians withdrew. In the central hill country, hundreds of small farming villages appeared, without pig bones, with simple houses and storage pits. Many archaeologists identify these as early Israel.

How does the book of Joshua relate to this evidence? Opinions vary widely. Older scholars (W. F. Albright) saw a military conquest matching the destruction layers. Others proposed peaceful infiltration of nomads (Albrecht Alt) or a peasant revolt within Canaan (George Mendenhall, Norman Gottwald). Today many archaeologists, such as Israel Finkelstein and William Dever, think Israel emerged mostly from within Canaan. Conservative scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen and Richard Hess argue that the book itself describes a limited campaign: it says only three cities were burned (Jericho, Ai and Hazor, Josh 11:13), that much land remained unconquered (Josh 13:1), and that Canaanites still lived among Israel (Josh 15:63; Judg 1:27-33).

Specific sites are debated. At Jericho, John Garstang (1930s) dated a destroyed city to about 1400 BC; Kathleen Kenyon (1950s) redated that destruction to about 1550 BC and found little Late Bronze occupation; Bryant Wood (1990) argued again for 1400 BC, and radiocarbon tests have generally supported Kenyon's earlier date. Ai (usually identified with et-Tell) seems to have been unoccupied in the Late Bronze Age, which has led some to propose another site. Hazor, by contrast, has a massive burned destruction layer of the 13th century BC.

The book's own shape follows Deuteronomy: a new Moses (Joshua), a new crossing of waters, circumcision and Passover at Gilgal, holy war against idolatry, a covenant ceremony on Mount Ebal (Josh 8:30-35, as Deut 27 commanded), land allotment and covenant renewal. In the 1980s Adam Zertal excavated a structure on Mount Ebal that he identified as an Israelite altar; others see it as a farmhouse or watchtower.

culture.explain: In ancient warfare a god was believed to fight for his people. Devoting a city to God (herem) meant giving it entirely to him, often by destruction, with no plunder. The Moabite king Mesha (9th century BC) boasts of doing the same to Israelite towns for his god Chemosh.

Ancient Near Eastern conquest accounts routinely used total language ('left none remaining') for victories that were partial. Joshua itself shows Canaanites still living in the land after such statements.
Stone heaps marked sacred events and served as teaching tools: 'when your children ask'. Twelve stones from the Jordan stand at Gilgal.
Land was distributed by casting lots before God, so that every tribe and clan received its share from God's hand, not by power. It could not be sold permanently.
The Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty. Even though it was deceptive, the oath made in God's name must be kept: covenant faithfulness binds even toward foreigners.
Shechem, where Abraham first built an altar, becomes the place where Joshua gathers all Israel to choose the LORD and set up a witness stone.

jewishLens:
In the Hebrew Bible Joshua opens the second division, the *Nevi'im* (Prophets), as the first of the 'Former Prophets'. Jewish tradition reads it as prophetic history: the story of how God's word to Moses came true. Its first chapter is read as the *haftarah* (prophetic reading) on Simchat Torah, right after Moses' death in Deuteronomy, so that the transition from Moses to Joshua is relived every year. Joshua 2 (the spies and Rahab) is the haftarah for the Torah portion about Moses' spies (Num 13-15), contrasting a failed reconnaissance with a faithful one.

The rabbis were struck by Rahab. In Talmudic tradition (Megillah 14b) she becomes a righteous convert who married Joshua and was the ancestor of priests and prophets, including Jeremiah and Huldah. Her confession that 'the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath' (Josh 2:11) is treated as one of the great professions of faith. The Talmud also warns against taking the conquest as a licence: later rabbis treated the commands concerning the seven Canaanite nations as no longer applicable, since those nations had ceased to exist (compare Mishnah Yadayim 4:4 on the mixing of nations by Sennacherib).

The first audience would hear Joshua as the fulfilment of the promise first given to Abraham. The book's climax is not a battle but the statement that 'there failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass' (Josh 21:45). Yet it ends with a warning and a choice: 'choose you this day whom ye will serve' (Josh 24:15). The land is a gift within a relationship, held only by loyalty, and the exiles who later read Joshua knew how real that warning was.

flow.label: Be strong and courageous
flow.detail: God commissions Joshua after Moses' death and promises his presence, calling him to meditate on the law.

flow.label: Rahab and the spies
flow.detail: A Canaanite prostitute hides Israel's spies, confesses faith in the LORD and is spared with her family.

flow.label: Crossing the Jordan
flow.detail: The river stops as the priests carry the ark in. Israel camps at Gilgal, is circumcised and keeps Passover; the manna ends.

flow.label: Jericho and Achan
flow.detail: Jericho falls after a seven-day procession. Achan's theft brings defeat at Ai, showing that Israel can become like the Canaanites.

flow.label: Campaigns south and north
flow.detail: Gibeon's treaty draws Israel into war with a southern coalition; then a northern coalition led by Hazor is defeated.

flow.label: Dividing the inheritance
flow.detail: The land is allotted to the tribes by lot, with cities of refuge and Levitical towns; Caleb receives Hebron.

flow.label: Choose whom to serve
flow.detail: Joshua's farewell and the covenant at Shechem: Israel promises to serve the LORD, and a stone is set up as witness.

keyWords.meaning: Something given wholly to God, usually by destruction, and forbidden for human use.
The family land allotted by God; the word occurs dozens of times in Joshua 13-21.
Settled peace from enemies in the land, a key promise of Deuteronomy.

keyWords.word: Be strong and of good courage
keyWords.meaning: The repeated charge to Joshua and to Israel, grounded in God's presence, not in human ability.
To worship and obey. The final chapter uses it again and again: serve the LORD, not the gods beyond the river.

connections.how: Joshua carries out Deuteronomy's commands: the covenant ceremony on Mount Ebal, cities of refuge, and destruction of idolatrous cities.
Judges opens after Joshua's death and shows how incomplete the occupation was and how quickly Israel turned to other gods.
The land given in Joshua is the land promised to Abraham; Joseph's bones are finally buried at Shechem.
Hebrews says Joshua did not give the final rest, which remains for God's people; it also commends Rahab's faith.
Rahab appears in Jesus' genealogy, a Canaanite woman in the line of the Messiah.
James cites Rahab as an example of faith shown in action.

jesusLens: The name Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua (*Yehoshua*, 'the LORD saves'); in Heb 4:8 the Greek actually reads 'Jesus' for Joshua. Christians have long read Joshua as a type of Jesus: a new leader after Moses who brings God's people into their inheritance. Hebrews says Joshua's rest was not final; a deeper Sabbath rest remains (Heb 4:8-11). Many Christian readers note that Jesus reverses the pattern of conquest: instead of taking land by the sword, he sends his followers to all nations with the message of peace (Matt 28:18-20), and the inheritance is widened to 'the meek' and the whole earth (Matt 5:5). Rahab, a Canaanite who sides with Israel's God, is included in Jesus' family tree (Matt 1:5), showing that faith, not ethnicity, defined membership even in Joshua. Jewish readers focus on the land as God's continuing gift to the Jewish people and on Joshua as the faithful disciple of Moses who received the Torah from him (Mishnah Avot 1:1).

misreadings.topic: The conquest as genocide or as a model for today
misreadings.popular: Readers tend to fall into one of two camps. One reads Joshua as a straightforward record of God commanding the extermination of whole peoples, which they either defend flatly or reject as proof the Old Testament God is cruel. The other has used Joshua to justify 'Christian' conquests, from crusades to colonial settlement.
misreadings.inContext: Scholars note that ancient war reports used sweeping, stereotyped language ('utterly destroyed all that breathed') for limited victories, and Joshua itself says Canaanites remained (Josh 13:1-6; Josh 15:63; Judg 1:21-36). Paul Copan, Matthew Flannagan and Nicholas Wolterstorff argue for hyperbole and that the targets were mainly military strongholds. The command was tied to a unique moment and to judgment on specific practices such as child sacrifice (Deut 12:31), not ethnicity: Canaanite Rahab is saved and Israelite Achan is destroyed. Jewish tradition already confined the commands to the past.
misreadings.defence: Traditional evangelical and Reformed scholars, such as Wayne Grudem and William Lane Craig in his earlier writing, hold that God, as giver of life and judge of all, could rightly command limited judgment on a corrupt culture after centuries of patience (Gen 15:16), and some warn that the hyperbole argument can be stretched too far to explain away the text. Others, such as Douglas Earl, read the stories mainly as theological symbolism about undivided loyalty. Nearly all agree that the commands were unique to that moment in salvation history and give no warrant for any war today.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Joshua has been misused to justify violence; reading it in context protects against that while still taking seriously God's judgment on evil and his inclusion of outsiders like Rahab.

misreadings.topic: Joshua 1:8 as a formula for personal success
misreadings.popular: Josh 1:8 promises that if you meditate on God's word daily you will be prosperous and successful in your career and plans.
misreadings.inContext: The words are spoken to Israel's leader at a specific moment: success means carrying out God's commission to bring Israel into the land in line with the Torah. The 'success' (Hebrew *sakal*, act wisely) is about wise, faithful leadership under God's word, like the king who reads the law daily in Deut 17:18-20.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical teachers rightly draw a general principle: those who soak in God's word grow in wisdom (Ps 1:1-3). Scholars on all sides agree the verse is about faithfulness to God's purposes, not a guarantee of personal ambition.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reading it as a career promise shrinks a call to covenant leadership into self-help.

relevance.then: Joshua told Israel that its land was God's gift, fulfilling his oath to Abraham; that holding it depended on covenant loyalty, not military power; and that outsiders who trust the LORD can be welcomed while insiders who betray him are judged.
relevance.now: Joshua raises hard questions about violence and judgment that readers must face honestly. It also speaks of God's faithfulness to every promise, courage grounded in God's presence, the danger of compromise, the inclusion of unlikely outsiders, and the need for every generation to choose whom it will serve.

oneLine: Judges shows Israel spiralling down after Joshua, crying out to God and being rescued by flawed deliverers again and again, until the nation is as broken as the Canaanites it replaced.

author.name: Unknown; Samuel by Jewish tradition; the Deuteronomistic historians (critical)
author.who: The Talmud (Baba Bathra 14b) names Samuel. The refrain 'in those days there was no king in Israel' suggests a writer who lived under the monarchy. Most critical scholars see Judges as part of the Deuteronomistic History, combining old hero stories with a theological framework.
author.howWeKnow: The book does not name its author. Its framework (sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance, rest) matches the language of Deuteronomy. Some stories contain very old material: the Song of Deborah (Judg 5) is widely regarded as among the oldest Hebrew poetry, perhaps 12th century BC. The note that the Danite priesthood lasted 'until the day of the captivity of the land' (Judg 18:30) suggests at least some editing after the fall of the north in 722 BC.

writtenFrom.note: The epilogue's negative picture of Benjamin and Gibeah (Saul's tribe and town) and its praise of Judah (Judg 1:1-2; Judg 20:18) suggest a writer sympathetic to David's house, possibly in the early monarchy, with later Deuteronomistic editing in Jerusalem.

writtenTo.who: Israel under the monarchy, and later the exiles
writtenTo.situation: Readers who knew kings, good and bad, needed to understand how Israel had fallen so far after Joshua, why it needed godly leadership, and why the real problem was not lack of a king but turning from the LORD. For exiles, Judges explained a pattern they had lived through: unfaithfulness leads to oppression, yet God still hears the cry.

setIn.note: From Joshua's death to the eve of Samuel and Saul. Early chronology: c. 1380-1050 BC; late chronology: c. 1200-1020 BC. Adding up the book's figures gives about 410 years, which is too long for either scheme, so most scholars think some judges overlapped as regional leaders. Jephthah's claim that Israel had held Transjordan for 300 years (Judg 11:26) is used by early-date supporters.

worldEvents.event: Ramesses III repels the Sea Peoples; the Philistines settle on the southern coast of Canaan and found five cities.
Egypt withdraws from Canaan, leaving a power vacuum filled by local peoples and tribes.
Iron working spreads; the Philistines guard their metal technology (compare 1 Sam 13:19-22).
Camel-riding raiders from the desert become a new threat, as with the Midianites in Gideon's story (Judg 6:5).
Shiloh, Israel's central sanctuary, is destroyed, probably by the Philistines (compare Jer 7:12).

backdrop:
The period of the judges falls in the early Iron Age, roughly the 12th and 11th centuries BC (or starting in the 14th century on the early chronology). This was a time of collapse and reshuffling across the Mediterranean. Egypt's empire in Canaan faded, the Philistines and other Sea Peoples settled the coast, and Israel lived as a loose federation of tribes in the hill country, without a capital, standing army or king. Each tribe faced local threats: Moabites to the east, Canaanite chariot cities in the valleys, Midianite camel raiders, Ammonites, and finally the Philistines.

The 'judges' (Hebrew *shofetim*) were not mainly courtroom judges. Most were charismatic military deliverers, raised up by God for a crisis, whom 'the Spirit of the LORD came upon' (Judg 3:10; Judg 6:34; Judg 14:6). Only Deborah is shown actually judging cases (Judg 4:4-5). Their authority was local and temporary, and they did not found dynasties; when Gideon is offered a crown he refuses, saying 'the LORD shall rule over you' (Judg 8:23), though his son Abimelech seizes kingship disastrously (Judg 9).

The book is carefully arranged. After a double introduction (Judg 1:1-3:6) it presents twelve judges, six major and six minor. The cycle repeats: Israel does evil, God hands them to an oppressor, they cry out, God raises a deliverer, the land has rest. But each cycle gets worse. Othniel is a model judge; Gideon ends by making an idol; Jephthah sacrifices his own daughter; Samson breaks every vow and fights only for personal revenge. Scholars such as Barry Webb and Daniel Block call this a downward spiral.

The last five chapters (Judg 17-21) are not about judges at all. They show a household idol shrine, a tribe that steals a priest and wipes out a peaceful town, a Levite whose concubine is gang-raped and murdered at Gibeah, in a scene deliberately echoing Sodom (Gen 19), and a civil war that nearly destroys Benjamin. The refrain frames it: 'every man did that which was right in his own eyes' (Judg 17:6; Judg 21:25). Israel has become Canaan.

culture.explain: A leader who delivers and governs, raised up by God in a crisis. Not a royal office and not inherited.
Sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance, rest, and back to sin. The pattern is laid out in Judg 2 and repeated through the book, each time worse.
Canaanite storm god and mother goddess, believed to bring rain and fertility. For farmers in a land dependent on rain, they were a constant temptation.
Ehud, a Benjaminite (the name means 'son of the right hand'), is left-handed, which lets him hide his sword on the unexpected side. Benjamin was known for left-handed slingers.
Protecting guests was a sacred duty. The horror at Gibeah lies partly in its betrayal of hospitality by Israelites, echoing Sodom.
Vows to God were binding and taken very seriously. Jephthah's rash vow ends in tragedy; the Torah offered ways to redeem persons vowed to God, which he does not use.
The book's women trace its moral decline: Achsah asks boldly for land, Deborah leads, Jael kills Sisera; later Jephthah's daughter, Samson's women and the Levite's concubine are victims.

jewishLens:
Judges is the second book of the *Nevi'im Rishonim* (Former Prophets), and Jewish tradition reads it as prophetic teaching rather than simple chronicle. Several haftarot come from it: the Song of Deborah (Judg 4:4-5:31) is read on Shabbat Shirah alongside the Song of the Sea, pairing Miriam's song with Deborah's; the birth of Samson (Judg 13) accompanies the Torah reading on the Nazirite (Num 4:21-7:89); and Jephthah's story (Judg 11:1-33) is read with the story of Israel's dealings with Sihon in Num 21. The rabbis loved Deborah as a prophetess and judge, though some also commented on her calling herself 'a mother in Israel' (Judg 5:7) as a sign of strong leadership.

The rabbis were troubled by Jephthah. A midrash (Genesis Rabbah 60:3; Leviticus Rabbah 37:4) says his vow was invalid and that the high priest Phinehas could have released him, but both were too proud to go to the other; so a daughter died through two men's pride. The verdict is that the Torah never wanted this. Gideon's refusal of kingship (Judg 8:23) became a classic text for the idea that God alone is Israel's king.

The first audience, living under kings, would have heard Judges as a mirror. The problem was not simply that there was no king; it was that Israel 'forgat the LORD their God' (Judg 3:7) and that each person did what was right in their own eyes. Yet even in this dark book God keeps hearing his people's cry. When Israel finally repents and puts away its gods, 'his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel' (Judg 10:16). The covenant relationship holds, not because Israel deserves it, but because God refuses to let his people go.

flow.label: Incomplete conquest
flow.detail: Tribes fail to drive out the Canaanites and settle down beside them. A new generation arises that does not know the LORD.

flow.label: The cycle explained
flow.detail: The narrator lays out the pattern of apostasy, oppression, crying out and deliverance that the book will follow.

flow.label: Early judges
flow.detail: Othniel is a model deliverer; Ehud assassinates the Moabite king; Deborah, Barak and Jael defeat Sisera's chariots.

flow.label: Gideon and Abimelech
flow.detail: A fearful Gideon defeats Midian with 300 men but makes an ephod that Israel worships. His son Abimelech murders his brothers to become king.

flow.label: Jephthah's tragic vow
flow.detail: An outcast becomes leader against Ammon, but his rash vow costs his daughter's life, and he fights a civil war with Ephraim.

flow.label: Samson's wasted strength
flow.detail: A Nazirite from birth, Samson follows his eyes, breaks his vows and is captured, yet in death he brings down the temple of Dagon.

flow.label: Israel becomes Canaan
flow.detail: Private idols, a stolen priesthood, the atrocity at Gibeah and near-genocide of Benjamin show total collapse.

keyWords.meaning: To govern, bring justice and rescue. The judges are deliverers who set things right.

keyWords.word: Evil in the eyes of the LORD
keyWords.meaning: The book's verdict formula, set against the closing 'right in his own eyes': whose eyes decide?
A cry of distress for help, the same as Israel's cry in Egypt. God responds to it even without full repentance.
God's empowering presence that 'comes upon' or 'rushes upon' judges for a task, not a sign of their moral maturity.
To rescue or give victory. Judges are often called 'saviours'; the root is in the names Joshua and Jesus.

connections.how: Judges picks up after Joshua's death and shows the failure to finish what Joshua began.
Ruth is set 'in the days when the judges ruled' and offers a bright counter-story of faithful kindness in Bethlehem.
Samuel is the last judge; the call for a king grows out of the chaos Judges describes.
The outrage at Gibeah is written to echo Sodom, showing that Israel has become what God judged.
Hebrews lists Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah among those who acted by faith.
Hosea recalls 'the days of Gibeah' as a byword for Israel's deep corruption.

jesusLens: Judges creates a longing for a true deliverer and a good king who will not fail. Christian readers have seen in the judges dim outlines of Christ: a saviour raised up by God, empowered by the Spirit, who rescues his people from oppression. Samson, who in his death defeats more enemies than in his life (Judg 16:30), has often been read as a flawed type of Christ's victory through death. The contrast is equally important: where the judges grow more selfish, Jesus gives himself for others; where 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes', Jesus does what is right in God's eyes (John 8:29). Jewish readers often read the book's ending as pointing to the need for the house of David and, in later hope, for the messianic king. Both traditions agree that Judges itself does not solve the problem; it shows the need.

misreadings.topic: The judges as moral heroes
misreadings.popular: Sunday school and sermons often present Gideon, Samson and Jephthah as heroes of faith to imitate: brave men God used because they trusted him.
misreadings.inContext: The book presents most judges as increasingly flawed: Gideon tests God repeatedly, takes revenge, and makes an ephod that becomes a snare (Judg 8:27); Jephthah's vow is tragic; Samson breaks every part of his Nazirite vow. Scholars such as Daniel Block, Barry Webb and Lillian Klein read the book as a critique of leadership and of Israel's 'Canaanization'. God uses them in spite of themselves.
misreadings.defence: Hebrews 11:32 does list Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah as people of faith, and evangelical scholars such as Webb note that Hebrews highlights the moment each trusted God, not their whole lives. Both sides agree: they had real faith at key moments, and the book also exposes their sins. The Bible's heroes are sinners used by grace.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reading the judges as simple role models misses the book's warning about leaders who use God's gifts for themselves, and its call for a better leader.

misreadings.topic: Gideon's fleece as a model for guidance
misreadings.popular: Christians are encouraged to 'put out a fleece': ask God for a sign to confirm a decision, as Gideon did.
misreadings.inContext: Gideon had already been told clearly what God wanted (Judg 6:14-16) and had seen a miraculous sign (Judg 6:21). The fleece tests come from fear and doubt, and Gideon himself apologises: 'Let not thine anger be hot against me' (Judg 6:39). The story shows God's patience with a frightened man, not a recommended method.
misreadings.defence: Some evangelical writers say God may still graciously confirm decisions, and that Gideon's request was answered. Most scholars, including those in the Reformed tradition such as Dale Ralph Davis, agree that the passage describes God's kindness to weakness rather than prescribing fleeces.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Seeing the fleece as weakness rather than method encourages trust in what God has already made clear.

relevance.then: Judges explained to Israel how quickly faith can fade in one generation, how compromise with surrounding culture corrupts, and how even God-given leaders can turn selfish. It also assured them that God hears the cry of his people, even when their repentance is shallow.
relevance.now: Judges is uncomfortably modern: moral relativism ('right in his own eyes'), leaders who use power for themselves, violence against women, and religion bent to private ends. It warns churches about cultural drift and celebrity leaders, and it keeps hope alive that God still rescues.

oneLine: Ruth is a short story of loyal love in which a grieving widow and her Moabite daughter-in-law find redemption through a generous kinsman, and become ancestors of King David.

author.name: Anonymous (Samuel by Jewish tradition)
author.who: The Talmud (Baba Bathra 14b) credits Samuel. Most scholars treat the author as unknown, a skilled storyteller writing in classical Hebrew. Some have suggested the story preserves a woman's perspective because women drive the plot, but there is no direct evidence of the author's gender.
author.howWeKnow: The book explains an old custom 'in former time' (Ruth 4:7), so it was written some time after the events. The genealogy ends with David (Ruth 4:17-22), so it was written in or after his time. Scholars split between a monarchy date (based on the Hebrew style and interest in David's ancestry) and a post-exilic date (reading it as a quiet answer to the ban on foreign wives in Ezra 9-10 and Neh 13).

writtenFrom.note: The story is set in and around Bethlehem; the writer knows its customs, fields and town gate. Coordinates are for Bethlehem.

writtenTo.who: Israel, either under David's dynasty or after the exile
writtenTo.situation: If written under the monarchy, Ruth explains and defends David's family line, including his Moabite great-grandmother. If written after the exile, it reminds a community anxious about outsiders that a Moabite woman who chose Israel's God became the ancestor of its greatest king.

setIn.note: Set 'in the days when the judges ruled' (Ruth 1:1). Since Boaz is David's great-grandfather and David was born c. 1040 BC, the story falls roughly in the late 12th or early 11th century BC, though the genealogy may skip generations. The narrative itself covers about ten years in Moab (Ruth 1:4) and then one harvest season.

worldEvents.event: Egypt's control of Canaan ends; local peoples like Moab grow in strength.
Famines and drought in the eastern Mediterranean contribute to migrations at the end of the Bronze Age.
Philistine pressure on Israel's hill country increases.
The Mesha Stele shows Moab as a kingdom with its own god Chemosh, long a rival of Israel.
Ezra and Nehemiah oppose marriages with Moabites and others; some scholars think Ruth was written or read in this setting.

backdrop:
Ruth is set in the same dark period as Judges, but it reads like a different world. Instead of war and idolatry, we see a farming town, harvest fields, a threshing floor and a town gate where elders meet. A famine drives Elimelech, his wife Naomi and their two sons from Bethlehem (which means 'house of bread') to Moab. The sons marry Moabite women. Then all three men die, leaving three widows with no sons.

In that world a widow without sons was in danger. Land and inheritance passed through men; a woman's security depended on husband, sons or male relatives. Israel's law tried to protect such people. Farmers had to leave the edges of their fields and the dropped stalks for 'the poor and the stranger' to glean (Lev 19:9-10; Deut 24:19). A close relative, the *go'el* (redeemer), was responsible for buying back family land sold in poverty (Lev 25:25) and for protecting family members. In the levirate custom, a dead man's brother married his widow to give him an heir (Deut 25:5-10). Ruth weaves these customs together, though the exact legal arrangements in Ruth 4 are debated, since Boaz is not a brother.

Ruth is a Moabite, and that matters. Moab was Israel's neighbour and rival, born, according to Genesis, from Lot's incest with his daughter (Gen 19:30-38). Deuteronomy says no Moabite shall enter the assembly of the LORD 'even to their tenth generation' (Deut 23:3), because Moab refused Israel bread and hired Balaam to curse them. Yet this Moabite woman shows more covenant loyalty than anyone in Judges. Later rabbis resolved the tension by reading the law as applying to Moabite men only (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3).

The book is a masterpiece of storytelling, built in four scenes: emptiness in Moab, a meeting in the field, a night at the threshing floor, and a legal settlement at the gate. Names carry meaning: Naomi ('pleasant') asks to be called Mara ('bitter') (Ruth 1:20); her sons Mahlon and Chilion sound like 'sickness' and 'wasting'; the nearer kinsman is left nameless, called in Hebrew 'so-and-so' (Ruth 4:1), because he refuses to preserve a name.

culture.explain: The poor, widows and foreigners had a legal right to gather what reapers missed. Boaz goes beyond the law, telling his workers to drop extra stalks for Ruth.
A close relative with the duty to buy back family land, free relatives from debt-slavery and protect the family name.
A brother marries his dead brother's widow to raise an heir in the dead man's name. Ruth combines this idea with redemption of land.

An open, flat area where grain was separated at harvest. Men often slept there to guard the grain. It could have associations with festivity and sexual license (compare Hos 9:1), which gives the night scene its tension.

Ruth asks Boaz to 'spread thy skirt over thine handmaid', literally 'spread your wing', a request for marriage and protection (compare Ezek 16:8). It echoes Boaz's own blessing on her, taking refuge under God's wings.
Handing over a sandal sealed a transfer of property rights; the narrator explains it as an old custom.

jewishLens:
Ruth is one of the five *Megillot* (scrolls) read on festivals, and it is read on Shavuot, the feast of weeks, which celebrates both the wheat harvest and the giving of the Torah at Sinai. Tradition gives several reasons: the story takes place at harvest time (Ruth 1:22; Ruth 2:23); Ruth's choice to join Israel ('thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God', Ruth 1:16) mirrors Israel accepting the Torah at Sinai; and by tradition David, Ruth's descendant, was born and died on Shavuot. Ruth is the model convert in Jewish law, and her words to Naomi shape the classic conversion process: the rabbis read each phrase as acceptance of a part of Jewish life (Yevamot 47b).

The midrash Ruth Rabbah observes that the scroll contains no laws of purity or impurity, of permitted or forbidden, and asks why it was written; its answer is: to teach how great is the reward of those who do acts of loving-kindness (*gemilut hasadim*). The key Hebrew word *hesed* (loyal, covenant love) appears three times (Ruth 1:8; Ruth 2:20; Ruth 3:10) and drives the whole book. Naomi blesses her daughters-in-law for their hesed; Boaz praises Ruth's hesed; and God's own hesed works quietly through their kindness. God acts directly only twice in the narrator's voice: giving bread (Ruth 1:6) and giving conception (Ruth 4:13).

For a first audience the point would be clear: covenant faithfulness is not only about bloodline. A foreign widow who binds herself to Israel's God, people and land by loyal love can become part of the family, and even the mother of kings. In the Hebrew Bible Ruth often follows Proverbs in the Writings, so that Ruth, whom Boaz calls 'a virtuous woman' (*eshet chayil*, Ruth 3:11), appears right after the poem of the 'virtuous woman' (Prov 31:10). She is that ideal in action.

flow.label: Famine and loss
flow.detail: Naomi's family flees famine to Moab. Her husband and both sons die, leaving three widows.

flow.label: Ruth's oath of loyalty
flow.detail: Orpah returns home; Ruth refuses to leave Naomi and binds herself to her people and God.

flow.label: Return empty to Bethlehem
flow.detail: Naomi arrives bitter, saying the LORD brought her back empty, just as barley harvest begins.

flow.label: Gleaning in Boaz's field
flow.detail: Ruth 'happens' to glean in the field of Boaz, a relative, who treats her with generous protection.

flow.label: Night at the threshing floor
flow.detail: On Naomi's plan, Ruth asks Boaz to spread his wing over her as redeemer. He praises her loyalty and promises to act.

flow.label: Redemption at the gate
flow.detail: The nearer kinsman declines; Boaz redeems the land and marries Ruth before the elders.

flow.label: A son for Naomi
flow.detail: Obed is born; the women say Naomi has a son. The genealogy runs to David.

keyWords.meaning: Faithful, generous love within a relationship, going beyond what is required. The theme of the whole book.
A family protector who buys back land or people; the root appears over 20 times in Ruth.
To turn back or come home; used of Naomi's return and, paradoxically, of Ruth 'returning' to a land she has never seen.
The wing of a bird or the corner of a garment. God's wings shelter Ruth; she asks Boaz to spread his.
Strength, worth, capability. Boaz is a man of worth (Ruth 2:1); Ruth is a woman of worth (Ruth 3:11).

connections.how: Set in the same era, Ruth contrasts sharply with Judges' violence; both have a Levite or a family from Bethlehem at their centre.
The blessing at the gate links Ruth with Rachel, Leah and Tamar, other women who built Israel's house through unconventional paths.
Ruth puts Deuteronomy's laws for the widow, stranger and levirate marriage into action, and tests its exclusion of Moabites.
Ruth ends with David's name, leading into the books of Samuel where David rises to power.
In the Hebrew order Ruth follows Proverbs; she embodies the 'woman of worth' of Prov 31.
Ruth is one of four women named in Jesus' genealogy, all with foreign or irregular stories.

jesusLens: Matthew names Ruth in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:5), alongside Tamar, Rahab and 'her that had been the wife of Urias', suggesting that the Messiah's family has always included outsiders and unexpected stories. Christian readers have long seen Boaz as a picture of Christ the kinsman-redeemer, who must be a relative (compare Heb 2:14-17), able and willing to pay, and who takes a foreign bride under his protection. The phrase 'spread thy skirt' recalls the image of God as Israel's husband (Ezek 16:8) and of the church as Christ's bride. Jewish readers emphasise Ruth as the ancestor of David and so of the Messiah (the Targum on Ruth expands the genealogy with messianic hope), and as the model convert whose hesed the whole community should copy. Both traditions see in Ruth a God who works through ordinary faithfulness rather than miracles.

misreadings.topic: Ruth as a romance and dating guide
misreadings.popular: Ruth is a love story: a godly young woman waits patiently, a godly man notices her, and they marry. Christian books have used Ruth and Boaz as a model for dating and 'waiting for your Boaz'.
misreadings.inContext: The story is less about romance than about survival, loyalty and redemption. Its central relationship is Ruth's commitment to Naomi, an older widow; the marriage serves to preserve a dead man's name and restore a family's land. Ruth takes bold initiative at the threshing floor, and Boaz acts out of covenant duty and admiration for her hesed. Scholars such as Robert Hubbard, Tikva Frymer-Kensky and Katharine Doob Sakenfeld stress the social and legal setting.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical commentators such as Daniel Block and Iain Duguid agree, while noting that the book does present a beautiful marriage built on character and faithfulness, which is a legitimate application. The disagreement is mostly between popular devotional use and the book's own focus, not between scholarly camps.
misreadings.whyItMatters: Reducing Ruth to romance misses its radical themes: a foreigner welcomed, a widow restored and God's kindness working through community.

misreadings.topic: What happened at the threshing floor
misreadings.popular: Readers either assume Ruth's night visit was entirely innocent, or (in some modern readings) that it was a seduction with sexual relations implied by 'uncover his feet'.
misreadings.inContext: The language is deliberately suggestive: 'feet' can be a euphemism in Hebrew, and the threshing floor had loose associations. Most scholars, including Jewish and evangelical commentators, conclude that the narrator builds tension and then shows both Ruth and Boaz acting honourably: Boaz praises her virtue, protects her reputation and settles the matter legally the next morning (Ruth 3:10-14).
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars generally hold the honourable reading; some feminist and critical scholars argue for a sexual encounter. The text's own judgment, through Boaz, is that Ruth is a woman of worth, which supports the honourable reading.
misreadings.whyItMatters: The scene shows how loyalty and integrity act in a risky situation, and how a vulnerable woman was protected rather than exploited.

relevance.then: Ruth showed Israel that covenant faithfulness is lived in fields and family obligations, that the law's provisions for the poor were meant to be practised generously, and that a foreigner who trusts Israel's God belongs, even in the royal line.
relevance.now: Ruth speaks to refugees, widows, mixed families and people who feel empty and bitter. It honours loyalty across generations and cultures, models generous employers and neighbours, and shows that God's quiet providence often works through ordinary kindness.

oneLine: 1 Samuel tells how Israel moved from judges to kings: God raises the prophet Samuel, grants a king the people demand, rejects Saul for disobedience and chooses the shepherd boy David.

author.name: Unknown; Samuel, Nathan and Gad by tradition; Deuteronomistic historians (critical)
author.who: The Talmud (Baba Bathra 15a) says Samuel wrote the book up to his death and the prophets Nathan and Gad completed it, based on 1 Chr 29:29. Critical scholars see Samuel as part of the Deuteronomistic History, built from earlier sources.
author.howWeKnow: Samuel's death is recorded in 1 Sam 25:1, so he could not have written all of it. The phrase 'unto this day' (1 Sam 5:5; 1 Sam 27:6) and the note that Ziklag belonged to 'the kings of Judah' (1 Sam 27:6) suggest writing after the kingdom divided. Scholars have identified source blocks: the Ark Narrative (1 Sam 4-6 with 2 Sam 6) and the History of David's Rise (1 Sam 16 to 2 Sam 5). The Hebrew text of Samuel has many difficulties; the Dead Sea Scrolls copy 4QSam-a often agrees with the Greek Septuagint against the standard Hebrew text.
otherWritings: 2 Samuel (one book in the Hebrew Bible)

writtenFrom.note: Probably compiled in Jerusalem from early court and prophetic sources, perhaps beginning in the united monarchy, and edited in the late monarchy and exile.

writtenTo.who: Israel under the house of David, and later the exiles
writtenTo.situation: Readers needed to know why David's family, not Saul's, held the throne, and what kind of king God wants. For exiles who had lost their king, the book asked what went wrong with monarchy and whether God's choice of David still held.

setIn.note: From Samuel's birth to Saul's death at Mount Gilboa. Approximate dates: Samuel born c. 1105 BC, Saul's reign c. 1050-1010 BC (Acts 13:21 gives 40 years; the Hebrew of 1 Sam 13:1 is damaged and gives no clear number). Some minimalist scholars doubt that Saul and David ruled more than small chiefdoms; the Tel Dan Stele (9th century BC), naming the 'house of David', confirms at least that David founded a known dynasty.

worldEvents.event: Philistine cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath) dominate the coast; their distinctive pottery and temple architecture spread inland.
Shiloh is destroyed; its priesthood relocates to Nob.
Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified town in the Elah Valley (where David fought Goliath), is built and occupied; its excavator links it to early Judah.
An ostracon from Gath (Tell es-Safi) bears names similar to Goliath, showing such non-Semitic names were used there.
The Tel Dan Stele, written by an Aramean king, mentions the 'house of David'.

backdrop:
1 Samuel opens in the last chaotic years of the judges. The tabernacle stands at Shiloh, but its priests, Eli's sons Hophni and Phinehas, are corrupt, taking the best of the sacrifices and sleeping with the women who serve at the entrance (1 Sam 2:12-17; 1 Sam 2:22). The greatest threat is the Philistines, a people from the Aegean world who settled on the coast around 1175 BC. They had organised city-states, chariots, iron weapons and a monopoly on metalworking (1 Sam 13:19-22). Israel, a loose tribal league, could not match them.

When Israel takes the ark into battle like a lucky charm, the Philistines capture it and destroy Shiloh's power (1 Sam 4). Eli's daughter-in-law names her son Ichabod, 'where is the glory?', for 'the glory is departed from Israel' (1 Sam 4:21). But the ark humiliates the Philistine god Dagon and brings plague, until the Philistines send it back (1 Sam 5-6). The message: Israel's God cannot be controlled, and he fights his own battles.

The demand for a king (1 Sam 8) comes from real pressures: Samuel's sons are corrupt, and the Philistine threat needs a permanent army. But the people want a king 'like all the nations' (1 Sam 8:5, 1 Sam 8:20). God tells Samuel 'they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them' (1 Sam 8:7), yet he grants the request and chooses Saul. Scholars have long noted that the book contains both pro-monarchy and anti-monarchy strands (compare 1 Sam 9:15-17 with 1 Sam 8:10-18). The resolution is that kingship is acceptable if the king and people obey the LORD (1 Sam 12:13-15).

Saul starts well but fails when he offers sacrifice without waiting for Samuel (1 Sam 13:8-14) and keeps the spoils of Amalek (1 Sam 15). Samuel's verdict, 'to obey is better than sacrifice' (1 Sam 15:22), becomes a key prophetic theme. God sends Samuel to anoint David, the youngest son of Jesse in Bethlehem, because 'the LORD looketh on the heart' (1 Sam 16:7). The rest of the book traces the rise of David and the slow, tragic decline of Saul, who hunts David in jealousy while David refuses to harm 'the LORD's anointed' (1 Sam 24:6; 1 Sam 26:9). Many scholars read these chapters as an 'apology' defending David against the charge that he usurped Saul's throne.

culture.explain: Hannah's childlessness brings shame and taunting from her rival wife. She vows that if God gives her a son, he will be dedicated to God as a lifelong Nazirite.
The ark was the footstool of the invisible God 'which dwelleth between the cherubims'. Taking it into battle treated God as a tool; he would not be used.
Pouring oil on the head set a person apart for a God-given office. The 'anointed one' (Hebrew mashiach) became a title for the king.

In some ancient (and Aegean) traditions, a battle could be decided by single combat between champions representing their armies. Goliath's challenge follows this pattern, and his armour is described in Aegean style.
Jonathan makes a covenant with David, gives him his robe and weapons (symbols of his status as heir), and they swear loyalty for their descendants.
Consulting the dead through a medium was common in the ancient Near East and forbidden in Israel. Saul himself had banned it, then sought it in desperation.

jewishLens:
In the Hebrew Bible, 1 and 2 Samuel form a single book among the Former Prophets. Its opening has a special place in Jewish worship: the story of Hannah and her prayer (1 Sam 1:1-2:10) is the haftarah read on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, the New Year, because tradition says God 'remembered' Sarah, Rachel and Hannah on that day. The Talmud (Berakhot 31a) learns the laws of prayer from Hannah: she spoke in her heart, only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard (1 Sam 1:13). That is why the central Jewish prayer, the Amidah, is said quietly, with moving lips. Hannah's song, celebrating a God who brings down the mighty and lifts the poor (1 Sam 2:1-10), is one of the great theological poems of the Bible.

Samuel himself is honoured as a prophet equal to Moses and Aaron (Ps 99:6; Jer 15:1). He is the last judge and the first of the great prophets who anointed kings and confronted them. Jewish tradition is honest about Saul: the rabbis note that Saul was tall and humble at first (1 Sam 9:21; 1 Sam 10:22), and some say he lost the kingdom for one sin while David kept it despite many, because David repented sincerely while Saul made excuses (Yoma 22b discusses this contrast).

The first audience would hear 1 Samuel as a story about who truly rules Israel. Kings may be anointed, but the LORD remains Israel's King. The covenant relationship is not cancelled by the monarchy; the king must listen to God's word through the prophet. Hannah's song sets the tone: 'The LORD maketh poor, and maketh rich: he bringeth low, and lifteth up' (1 Sam 2:7). The proud priests fall, the barren woman sings, the tall king fails and the youngest shepherd is chosen.

flow.label: Hannah's prayer answered
flow.detail: A barren woman pours out her heart at Shiloh, receives a son and gives him back to God, singing of a God who lifts the lowly.

flow.label: Samuel called, Eli's house judged
flow.detail: God calls the boy Samuel by night and announces judgment on Eli's corrupt sons.

flow.label: The ark captured and returned
flow.detail: Israel loses the ark to the Philistines; it defeats Dagon and returns on its own. Samuel leads Israel in repentance and victory.

flow.label: A king like the nations
flow.detail: Israel demands a king; Samuel warns of the cost, and God grants Saul, who is anointed and proclaimed.

flow.label: Saul rejected
flow.detail: Saul's impatience and partial obedience lead God to reject him: obedience is better than sacrifice.

flow.label: David anointed, Goliath defeated
flow.detail: The youngest son is chosen for his heart, and he defeats the Philistine champion in the name of the LORD.

flow.label: Saul hunts David
flow.detail: Jonathan protects David; David flees and twice spares Saul's life, refusing to seize the throne.

flow.label: Saul's end at Gilboa
flow.detail: Saul consults a medium, hears his doom and dies with his sons in battle against the Philistines.

keyWords.meaning: One anointed with oil for an office, especially the king. Translated into Greek as *christos*.
Ruler. The question of the book is whether a human king can rule without displacing God as King.
The inner person: will, motive and loyalty. God looks on the heart, not appearance.
Weight, honour, presence. Ichabod means 'no glory'. God honours those who honour him.
To hear and obey. Samuel's name is linked to God hearing; Saul fails because he does not listen.

connections.how: Samuel is the last judge, and the cry for a king arises from the chaos of the judges period.
Deuteronomy's law of the king foresees Israel asking for a king like the nations and sets limits that Saul fails.
Several psalms are linked by their headings to episodes in David's flight from Saul.
Mary's song echoes Hannah's song: God lifts the lowly and humbles the mighty.
Paul's sermon in Antioch traces history from Samuel and Saul to David and then to Jesus.
Jesus defends his disciples by citing David eating the holy bread at Nob.

jesusLens: 1 Samuel introduces the word 'anointed' (Hebrew *mashiach*, Greek *christos*) as a royal title: Hannah's song ends by saying God will 'exalt the horn of his anointed' (1 Sam 2:10) before Israel even has a king. The New Testament identifies Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of David. Mary's song (Luke 1:46-55) is modelled on Hannah's, presenting the birth of Jesus as the climax of the God who lifts the lowly. David, the overlooked youngest son from Bethlehem who defeats Israel's enemy as their representative, became a pattern for the Messiah. Christian readers have seen David's battle with Goliath as a picture of Christ fighting as his people's champion, though they caution against allegorising every detail. Jewish readers likewise trace messianic hope to David, while focusing on Samuel's model of prophetic integrity and Hannah's model of prayer.

misreadings.topic: David and Goliath as 'defeat your giants'
misreadings.popular: The story teaches believers to face their personal 'giants' (fear, debt, illness, problems) with courage and faith, as David did; you are David, and with God you can win.
misreadings.inContext: In context the issue is the honour of Israel's God and his anointed king. Goliath defies 'the armies of the living God' (1 Sam 17:26), and David fights so that 'all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel' and that 'the battle is the LORD's' (1 Sam 17:46-47). David acts as Israel's representative champion: when he wins, the whole army shares the victory. The story also contrasts David with Saul, Israel's tall king who should have fought. Scholars and preachers such as Graeme Goldsworthy, Tim Keller and Robert Alter emphasise this representative and theological reading.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical preachers rightly draw lessons of courage and trust in God, which the text models (1 Sam 17:37). Commentators such as Dale Ralph Davis accept application while warning against making the reader the hero. Both sides agree that the main point is God's power through his chosen king, and that application should flow from that.
misreadings.whyItMatters: When readers cast themselves as David, the story becomes self-help. Read as Israel did, it points to God's victory through a representative champion, which shapes how Christians read the gospel.

misreadings.topic: Saul's sin as a minor technicality
misreadings.popular: Readers sometimes feel God was unfair to Saul: he only offered a sacrifice early and kept some animals for worship, while David committed adultery and murder but kept his throne.
misreadings.inContext: The book presents Saul's failures as a pattern of not listening to God's word through the prophet, which in Israel's covenant structure meant the king placing himself above God's rule. Saul blames the people and makes excuses (1 Sam 13:11-12; 1 Sam 15:20-21), while David, when confronted, confesses at once (2 Sam 12:13). Scholars such as Robert Gordon, Walter Brueggemann and David Gunn discuss Saul as a tragic figure; some see him as partly a victim of circumstances and of the narrative's pro-David bias.
misreadings.defence: Evangelical scholars generally hold that Saul's sins revealed a heart unwilling to submit to God and that the contrast with David is about repentance, not the size of the sin. They acknowledge the tragic sympathy the text shows Saul (1 Sam 31; 2 Sam 1:17-27).
misreadings.whyItMatters: The contrast teaches that God looks for a heart that listens and repents, not a flawless record.

relevance.then: 1 Samuel explained how Israel came to have kings, why David's line was God's choice, and that every king stands under God's word. It warned against using God's presence as a charm and showed that God lifts the humble and resists the proud.
relevance.now: 1 Samuel speaks about prayer in anguish, leadership under accountability, the danger of wanting to be 'like the nations', jealousy and insecurity in leaders, faithful friendship across rivalry, and God choosing people the world overlooks.

sources.author: Robert Alter
